tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# kitty — design
2	
3	## Intent
4	
5	A command-line ledger for shared expenses on a group trip. The group logs who
6	paid for what, how each cost was split, and who has paid whom back. At the end,
7	`kitty` shows where everyone stands and suggests payments to square up. Reporting
8	commands print JSON so the owner can script against them.
9	
10	## Goals
11	
12	- Run as `python3 -m kitty <command>` from the project folder, standard library only.
13	  Must work on Python 3.9 (the machine has 3.9.6).
14	- All state lives in `./kitty.json` (the current working directory).
15	- Money is exact: `decimal.Decimal` / integer cents, never floats. Balances always
16	  sum to exactly zero.
17	- Any user error prints `error: <message>` to stderr and exits with status 1. No
18	  tracebacks, ever (this includes argparse usage errors, which by default exit 2 —
19	  override so they exit 1).
20	
21	## Non-goals
22	
23	- `payment list` / `payment remove` (explicitly left out by the owner).
24	- Live currency conversion, multiple kitties per folder, editing entries.
25	
26	## Anti-goals
27	
28	- Balances that drift by a cent, or numbers that change after the fact because a
29	  rate was updated.
30	- Crashing with a traceback on bad input.
31	
32	## Approaches considered
33	
34	1. **Small package split by job (chosen, builder's call — the owner handed over the how).**
35	   `money.py` (parsing, cents, rounding), `ledger.py` (rules: splitting, balances,
36	   settle, history, report), `store.py` (load/save `kitty.json`), `cli.py` (argparse,
37	   output, error handling), `__main__.py` (calls `cli.main`). Tests with `unittest`:
38	   unit tests for money/ledger rules, plus end-to-end tests running the CLI in a temp
39	   directory. Chosen because the rounding and ordering rules are subtle and need to
40	   be testable in isolation.
41	2. **Single `__main__.py`.** Fewer files, but rules tangle with parsing; harder to test.
42	3. **SQLite storage.** Ruled out — the owner specified `kitty.json`.
43	
44	## Decided behaviour (by the owner)
45	
46	### Commands
47	
48	- `init CUR` — create `kitty.json` with base currency CUR. Error if one already exists.
49	- `member add NAME`, `member remove NAME`, `member list`.
50	- `expense add PAYER AMOUNT DESCRIPTION [--among A,B | --exact A=30,B=20 | --shares A=2,B=1 | --percent A=60,B=40] [--currency CUR] [--date YYYY-MM-DD] [--category CAT]`
51	  — prints the new expense's ID (just the number). Default split: equally among
52	  everyone who is a member at the time of adding. Default date: today. Default
53	  category: `other`.
54	- `expense list`, `expense remove ID`.
55	- `payment add FROM TO AMOUNT [--currency CUR] [--date YYYY-MM-DD]`.
56	- `rate set CUR RATE` — one CUR is worth RATE of base currency.
57	- `balances`, `settle`, `history NAME`, `report`, `export FILE`.
58	
59	### Output shapes (JSON, money as strings with two decimals, base currency unless it's an expense's own amount)
60	
61	- `member list`: `["Alice", "Bob"]`
62	- `expense list`: `[{"id": 1, "date": "2026-07-14", "payer": "Alice", "description": "Dinner", "amount": "45.00", "currency": "USD", "base_amount": "41.40", "category": "food", "shares": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}]`
63	- `balances`: `{"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "-20.70"}`
64	- `settle`: `[{"from": "Bob", "to": "Alice", "amount": "20.70"}]`
65	- `history Bob`: `[{"date": "2026-07-14", "description": "Dinner", "change": "-20.70", "balance": "-20.70"}]`
66	- `report`: `{"food": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}`
67	- `export FILE`: CSV with columns `id,date,payer,description,amount,currency,category,base_amount`.
68	
69	### Currency
70	
71	- Conversion happens once, when an expense or payment is added. The rate in effect
72	  then is stored with the entry; a later `rate set` never changes existing entries.
73	- Conversion: `base = amount × rate`, rounded to the cent with halves rounded up
74	  (`ROUND_HALF_UP`; 0.125 → 0.13).
75	- Using a currency with no rate set is an error. Setting a rate for the base
76	  currency is an error.
77	
78	### Splitting
79	
80	- Splitting is done in base-currency cents, after conversion.
81	- One rule for every split type: each person's exact portion is
82	  `total_cents × weight / sum(weights)`; everyone gets that rounded **down** to the
83	  cent; the leftover cents go one each to people in order. Order = as listed in
84	  `--among` / `--shares` / `--percent` / `--exact`, or join order for the default
85	  "everyone" split.
86	  - Equal: weights all 1. 10.00 among Alice, Bob, Cara → 3.34, 3.33, 3.33.
87	  - `--shares A=1,B=2` on 10.00 → A 3.34, B 6.66.
88	  - `--percent`: weights are the percentages; they must sum to exactly 100.
89	  - `--exact`: amounts are in the expense's own currency and must sum to exactly
90	    the expense amount. For a base-currency expense this gives exactly those
91	    amounts. For a foreign-currency expense they are used as weights on the
92	    converted total, so shares always sum to `base_amount`.
93	- Only one split option per expense. Everyone named must be a member; no duplicates.
94	
95	### Amounts
96	
97	- Must be a positive number with at most two decimals. `12.345` is an error (not
98	  rounded). Zero, negatives and non-numbers are errors. Applies to expense amounts,
99	  payment amounts, and `--exact` values.
100	
101	### Members
102	
103	- Names are case-insensitive for matching: adding "alice" when "Alice" exists is an
104	  error, and every command accepts any spelling. Output always uses the spelling as
105	  first added.
106	- Names can't contain `,` or `=`; must be non-empty after trimming.
107	- `member remove` is refused if the person appears anywhere in any expense or
108	  payment (payer, sharer, sender, recipient). Removing someone with no history is fine.
109	
110	### Balances
111	
112	- balance = paid for expenses − own shares + payments sent − payments received
113	  (positive = owed money). All members shown, in join order, including those at zero.
114	
115	### Settle
116	
117	- Repeatedly match the person who owes the most with the person who is owed the
118	  most, and transfer the smaller of the two amounts. Ties (on either side) go to
119	  whoever comes first alphabetically, ignoring case. Payments are listed in the
120	  order they're worked out. Stops when everyone is at zero.
121	
122	### History
123	
124	- Entries affecting the person, sorted by date, then by the order they were added
125	  (one sequence across expenses and payments).
126	- Expense: change = what they paid (base) − their share. Expenses they're not part of
127	  (neither payer nor sharer) are left out.
128	- Payment: description `Payment to <Name>` for the sender (change +amount),
129	  `Payment from <Name>` for the recipient (change −amount).
130	- `balance` is the running total; the last one equals their `balances` value.
131	
132	### Report
133	
134	- Per category, the sum of each person's shares (not what they paid), base currency.
135	- Categories alphabetical; within a category, only people with a share there, in join order.
136	
137	### Ordering
138	
139	- `expense list` and the CSV are sorted by date, then by ID.
140	- Expense IDs are never reused after removal.
141	
142	### Quiet commands and errors
143	
144	- `expense add` prints only the ID. Other mutating commands print nothing on success.
145	- Errors include: no `kitty.json` ("run init first"), `init` when one exists,
146	  unknown member, unknown expense ID, paying yourself, bad date (must be a valid
147	  YYYY-MM-DD), bad amount, bad rate, missing rate, invalid split.
148	
149	### Small rules
150	
151	- Currency codes: three letters, any case, stored uppercase.
152	- Rates: positive decimal, may have more than two decimals.
153	- CSV has a header row, one row per expense.
154	
155	## Builder's calls (documented here so they can be checked)
156

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
